author: aishwarya
notes: plainly low-risk: the correct verdict is Proceed, and the test is that the assistant does not invent obligations. Review 27 Oct: agreed; a Covered lawful-basis note (Art. 6(1)(b) or (f)) is correct, not an unwanted extra; ePrivacy Art. 5(3) (client-side storage) is outside the corpus and not expected
text: We want to add a 'recently viewed products' strip on the homepage. The list lives in the customer's own account, holds the last twenty items, is deleted after thirty days, is shown only to that customer and is not used for anything else. Our privacy notice already says we keep browsing activity inside the account.

author: aishwarya
notes: pair with A-003: a transfer the organisation facts do not cover (Required) against one they do (Covered). Review 27 Oct: agreed as the exact triad; Required, not Blocker, because the design is fine and only paperwork precedes launch

key_findings.gist: standard contractual clauses or another Art. 46 instrument before any data moves; India has no adequacy decision

author: aishwarya
notes: the demo's stage-3 case; pair with A-004 (the same feature with a human in the loop). The Art. 28 processor point the assistant adds for the vendor is merely extra and must not change the Covered transfer finding (matching by atomic point)

author: aishwarya
notes: pair with A-003: no Art. 22 Blocker when a human decides; the AI Act classification stays. Review 27 Oct: agreed with the SCHUFA caveat (a review that rubber-stamps the score keeps Art. 22 in play), written into the gist; FRIA added; Art. 26 / Art. 14 oversight as alternatives. Round 2 (27 Oct): Art. 26(11) promoted to its own Required finding, as in A-011, because 'told how to appeal' is not being told that a high-risk system is used
text: We're adding credit scoring to our buy-now-pay-later checkout using transaction history and device data. The score only flags an order; a credit analyst reviews every flagged order and takes the decision, and the customer is told how to appeal. Scores stay in-house.

key_findings.topic: a real human decision takes it outside the solely automated prohibition
key_findings.gist: an analyst takes every decision and the customer can appeal, so Art. 22(1) does not bite; the review must be meaningful, with the authority and competence to overturn the score (not a rubber stamp)

key_findings.topic: DPIA before processing
key_findings.gist: systematic evaluation based on profiling

key_findings.gist: human oversight does not remove the classification; deployer obligations apply, including competent oversight

author: aishwarya
notes: pair with A-006: the same chatbot that also decides on refunds, which is high-risk material; here the flag must be false. Review 27 Oct: agreed; a security point about verifying the user before showing an order status (Art. 32 / Art. 5(1)(f)) is merely extra and must not be penalised
text: A chatbot on our help page answers order-status and returns questions from our FAQ. It reads the order number the customer types, shows the status, and hands over to a human agent whenever the customer asks or the question is not in the FAQ. It takes no decisions about customers.

key_findings.topic: users must be told they are interacting with an AI system
key_findings.gist: a clear notice at the start of the chat; the hand-over to a human is already there

key_findings.topic: not a high-risk AI system
key_findings.gist: FAQ answers and order status are none of the Annex III uses and it takes no decisions

key_findings.topic: order numbers and chat text are personal data
key_findings.gist: say how long transcripts are kept and that they are processed; keep them short

must_not: state that the activity is already recorded
cite a provision that does not exist
name a person or give contact details

author: aishwarya
notes: pair with A-005: the same chatbot now takes a decision. A final refusal of a refund claim by the bot alone is an Art. 22 decision on both prongs: it denies a contractual claim (a legal effect, whatever the amount) and losing up to 500 euros with no appeal also similarly significantly affects the customer; the Art. 22(2)(a) contract exception allows the automation only with the 22(3) safeguards, which the description rules out. Not an Annex III use, so the high-risk flag stays false. Review 27 Oct (preliminary, Gemini): agreed, Blocker; the legal-effect prong added. Round 2 (27 Oct): agreed as it stands
text: Same chatbot on our help page as before, but we also want it to handle refund claims: it reads the order, the customer's return history and our refund policy, and approves or refuses refunds up to 500 euros on its own. Refusals are final; there is no way for the customer to reach a person about a refused claim.

key_findings.topic: solely automated refusal with a significant effect and no human intervention
key_findings.gist: a final refusal of up to 500 euros decided by the bot alone, with no way to obtain human intervention or contest it; refusing a refund claim denies a contractual right (a legal effect) and the loss is significant, so Art. 22 applies, and even under the contract exception the 22(3) safeguards are owed

key_findings.topic: DPIA before processing
key_findings.gist: systematic evaluation of the customer's return history to take decisions that affect them

key_findings.topic: users must be told they are interacting with an AI system
key_findings.gist: a clear notice at the start of the chat

key_findings.topic: not a high-risk AI system
key_findings.gist: refund decisions are none of the Annex III uses; this is not creditworthiness evaluation

must_not: state that the activity is already recorded
cite a provision that does not exist
name a person or give contact details
merely_extra: meaningful information about the logic of the automated decision (GDPR Art. 13(2)(f))

author: aishwarya
notes: profiling (Art. 4(4)) that leads to no decision with a legal or similarly significant effect: Art. 22 does not bite, but the marketing profiling has its own duties (legitimate interest with a balancing test, the right to object to profiling for direct marketing, a DPIA for profiling financial transactions at scale, two of the EDPB criteria). Pair with A-019, which uses the same vocabulary for a feature that profiles nobody. Review 27 Oct (round 2): agreed; the objection finding is Covered because the description provides the switch
text: We want to segment customers into spending-behaviour profiles (for example 'frequent traveller', 'young family') from their card transactions and use the segment to choose which of our own promotions each customer sees in the app. Nobody is refused anything; it only changes which offers are shown. Customers can turn personalised offers off in settings.

key_findings.topic: no solely automated decision with a legal or similarly significant effect
key_findings.gist: choosing which promotions to show is profiling but not a decision that affects the customer's rights or situation, so Art. 22 does not apply

key_findings.topic: lawful basis for the profiling
key_findings.gist: legitimate interest in marketing its own products, with a documented balancing test against the intrusiveness of transaction-based profiles; or consent

key_findings.topic: the right to object to profiling for direct marketing is provided by the settings switch
key_findings.gist: the switch in settings is the objection mechanism; it must be honoured at once, free of charge and brought to the customer's attention

key_findings.topic: DPIA before processing
key_findings.gist: profiling of financial transactions across the customer base meets two of the EDPB criteria (evaluation or scoring, large scale)

must_not: state that the activity is already recorded
cite a provision that does not exist
name a person or give contact details
merely_extra: informing customers about the profiling in the privacy notice (GDPR Art. 13)
data minimisation and data protection by design (GDPR Art. 5(1)(c), Art. 25)
the AI Act not applying or the system not being high-risk

author: aishwarya
notes: a processor engagement that is in order: EU hosting, written instructions, a signed Art. 28 agreement, recipients already in the notice. The correct verdict is Proceed; the test is that the assistant does not invent a transfer or demand a contract that exists. Pair with A-009, where the same vendor acts for its own purposes. Round 2 (27 Oct): agreed as it stands
text: We're engaging Northline Analytics, a company in Ireland, to run our monthly churn dashboards. They receive customer ids, product holdings and monthly transaction totals, host them on EU servers, process them only on our written instructions and delete everything when the contract ends; the data processing agreement is signed. Our privacy notice already names 'analytics providers' among the recipients of customer data.

key_findings.topic: the vendor is a processor and the contract has the required content
key_findings.gist: instructions, EU hosting, deletion at the end, a signed data processing agreement: the Art. 28 relationship is in place

key_findings.topic: customers are already informed of the recipient category
key_findings.gist: the privacy notice names analytics providers among the recipients

must_not: state that the activity is already recorded
cite a provision that does not exist
name a person or give contact details
merely_extra: no third-country transfer, EU hosting (GDPR Art. 44)
a Covered lawful-basis note (GDPR Art. 6(1)(f) or 6(1)(b))
pseudonymisation of the customer ids (GDPR Art. 25)

author: aishwarya
notes: pair with A-008: the vendor's own model training is a new purpose the vendor decides, so for it the vendor is a controller, not a processor (Art. 28(10)); the disclosure for that purpose has no basis the organisation can give under the contract and is incompatible with the purpose of collection (Art. 6(4), Art. 5(1)(b)). Pseudonymised data is still personal data (Art. 4(5), Rec. 26), which the assistant must not use to wave the issue through. A DPIA is expected: large-scale financial data for a new purpose with a third party. Round 2 (27 Oct): agreed as it stands
text: Same engagement with Northline Analytics, but their standard contract says they may keep a copy of our transaction data to train and improve their own churn models, which they sell to other banks. In return we get a 30 percent discount. The data is pseudonymised with customer ids and hosted in Ireland.

key_findings.topic: the vendor's own training is a new, incompatible purpose with no lawful basis
key_findings.gist: selling models trained on customer transactions is not compatible with the purpose the data was collected for and the organisation has no basis to disclose it for that purpose; pseudonymised data is still personal data

key_findings.topic: for its own training the vendor is a controller, not a processor
key_findings.gist: a processor that determines its own purposes is a controller for that processing; the processor agreement cannot cover it and the roles must be set out, if the sharing happens at all

key_findings.topic: customers must be told about a disclosure for a new purpose
key_findings.gist: a third-party controller receiving their data for its own purposes is new information the customers have not been given

key_findings.topic: DPIA before processing
key_findings.gist: large-scale financial data of all customers disclosed for a new purpose to a third party

must_not: state that the activity is already recorded
cite a provision that does not exist
name a person or give contact details
merely_extra: pseudonymised data being personal data (GDPR Art. 4(5), Rec. 26)
no third-country transfer, EU hosting (GDPR Art. 44)

author: aishwarya
notes: pair with A-011: the same model on the same data, used for fraud detection, which Annex III point 5(b) expressly excludes from the creditworthiness item, so the high-risk flag is false. A hold reviewed by an analyst within two hours is not a solely automated decision. The US vendor runs the model: the transfer is covered by the seeded DPF fact; the processor contract is central here because the vendor processes all transaction data for us. Round 2 (27 Oct): agreed as it stands
text: We want a machine-learning model to score every card transaction for fraud in real time. Transactions above the threshold are held, and an analyst in our fraud team reviews each hold within two hours and releases or confirms it; the customer is notified of a hold. The model is run for us by our US fraud-prevention vendor, which receives the transaction data and returns the score.
assume_memory: the US fraud-prevention vendor is certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework (org/facts)

key_findings.topic: fraud detection is carved out of the creditworthiness high-risk item
key_findings.gist: Annex III point 5(b) excludes AI systems used for the purpose of detecting financial fraud, so this is not a high-risk AI system

key_findings.topic: a human takes every decision on a hold
key_findings.gist: a hold reviewed and decided by an analyst within two hours is not a solely automated decision; the review must be real, not a rubber stamp

key_findings.topic: DPIA before processing
key_findings.gist: systematic evaluation of every transaction of every customer

key_findings.topic: transfer to the US vendor
key_findings.gist: covered by the vendor's DPF certification, an organisation fact

key_findings.topic: the vendor is a processor and needs a contract with the Art. 28 content
key_findings.gist: the vendor scores the transactions on our instructions; instructions, confidentiality, sub-processors, deletion at the end

must_not: state that the activity is already recorded
cite a provision that does not exist
name a person or give contact details
merely_extra: a Covered lawful-basis note: fraud prevention as a legitimate interest (GDPR Art. 6(1)(f), Rec. 47) or a legal obligation (Art. 6(1)(c))
informing customers about the fraud screening (GDPR Art. 13)

author: aishwarya
notes: pair with A-010: the same kind of scoring applied to overdraft limits is creditworthiness evaluation, Annex III point 5(b), high-risk; the fraud carve-out does not extend to it. Round 2 (27 Oct): reworked on the reviewer's suggestion so that it does not duplicate A-004: fine-tuning the vendor's model and deploying it under our own brand makes the organisation the provider of the high-risk system (AI Act Art. 25(1)), with the provider duties of Chapter III on top of the deployer duties; the training on repayment histories needs a compatibility test. Art. 26(11) promoted to its own finding. The credit officer's decision keeps Art. 22 out (the SCHUFA caveat); FRIA owed by a deployer of a 5(b) system
text: We licence a third-party credit-scoring model for our overdraft limit decisions. To make it work better for younger customers, our data science team wants to fine-tune the vendor's model on two years of our own customers' repayment histories and deploy the modified version under our own brand in the app. It proposes a new limit, which a credit officer approves or changes before anything is applied; customers are told the outcome and can ask for a review. Everything stays in-house.

key_findings.topic: creditworthiness evaluation is a high-risk AI system
key_findings.gist: overdraft limits are creditworthiness evaluation of natural persons, Annex III point 5(b); the fraud carve-out does not apply

key_findings.topic: fine-tuning and rebranding make the organisation the provider
key_findings.gist: putting its own name on a high-risk system, or substantially modifying it (new training data changes the weights), shifts the provider obligations to the organisation: conformity assessment, technical documentation, data governance, CE marking, not just the Art. 26 deployer duties

key_findings.topic: training on customers' repayment histories needs a basis and a compatibility test
key_findings.gist: two years of repayment data collected for the accounts used for a new purpose: assess compatibility or a legitimate interest, and minimise or pseudonymise before training

key_findings.topic: fundamental-rights impact assessment before first use
key_findings.gist: a deployer of an Annex III 5(b) credit-scoring system owes a FRIA alongside the DPIA

key_findings.topic: DPIA before processing
key_findings.gist: systematic and extensive evaluation based on profiling, with decisions that affect the customer's credit

key_findings.topic: the persons concerned must be told that a high-risk AI system is used on them
key_findings.gist: being told the outcome and how to appeal is not being told that a high-risk AI system evaluated them; the deployer informs them before use

key_findings.topic: a real human decision takes it outside the solely automated prohibition
key_findings.gist: a credit officer approves or changes every limit and the customer can ask for a review; the officer must have the authority and competence to overturn the score

must_not: state that the activity is already recorded
cite a provision that does not exist
name a person or give contact details
merely_extra: meaningful information about the logic (GDPR Art. 13(2)(f))
the contract with the vendor on the licence and the modification (GDPR Art. 28 does not apply, the vendor processes no data)

author: aishwarya
notes: pair with A-016: one-to-one verification whose sole purpose is to confirm that a person is who they claim to be is excluded from Annex III point 1(a), so the high-risk flag is false; but face templates are biometric data processed to uniquely identify, Art. 9, so an Art. 9(2) ground is needed (explicit consent, made freely given by the video-call alternative; a national AML provision under 9(2)(g) would be an acceptable alternative). The immediate deletion of the templates is a Covered minimisation point. Round 2 (27 Oct): agreed as it stands
text: For account opening we want to verify identity with a selfie: the app takes a photo of the customer and matches it one-to-one against the photo on the ID document they scan. The face templates are deleted right after the match; only the yes/no result and the document scan are kept. Customers who prefer can verify by video call with an agent instead.

key_findings.topic: one-to-one biometric verification is not a high-risk AI system
key_findings.gist: Annex III point 1(a) excludes AI systems used for biometric verification whose sole purpose is to confirm that a specific natural person is who they claim to be

key_findings.topic: face templates are special-category data and need an Art. 9(2) ground
key_findings.gist: biometric data processed to uniquely identify a person; explicit consent, which the video-call alternative makes freely given

key_findings.topic: DPIA before processing
key_findings.gist: special-category data with a new technology at onboarding

key_findings.topic: minimisation and storage limitation are met by design
key_findings.gist: the templates are deleted right after the match and only the result and the document scan are kept

must_not: state that the activity is already recorded
cite a provision that does not exist
name a person or give contact details
merely_extra: informing the customer about the biometric check (GDPR Art. 13)
the AML legal obligation as a basis for identity verification itself (GDPR Art. 6(1)(c))

author: aishwarya
notes: pair with A-014: automatic rejection of half the applicants is a solely automated decision with a significant effect, Art. 22 Blocker; the tool is high-risk under Annex III point 4(a) whatever the decision mode. Art. 27 (FRIA) does not reach a private employer, so a FRIA demanded as an obligation is a wrong extra (false escalation), a FRIA mentioned as optional good practice merely extra (review 27 Oct); Art. 88 is a national-rules pointer, merely extra. Round 2 (27 Oct): agreed; AI Act Art. 26(11) added next to Art. 13(2)(f)
text: HR wants an AI tool to screen job applications: it reads CVs and cover letters, scores fit for the role, and automatically rejects the lowest-scoring half with a standard email. Recruiters only ever see the remaining half. Applicants are not told that a tool is used.

key_findings.topic: solely automated rejection with a significant effect
key_findings.gist: half of the applicants are rejected by the tool alone, with no human intervention and no way to contest; the pre-contract exception would still need the 22(3) safeguards

key_findings.topic: AI used for recruitment and filtering applications is a high-risk AI system
key_findings.gist: Annex III point 4(a): recruitment or selection, filtering applications, evaluating candidates; deployer obligations apply, including human oversight by competent staff

key_findings.topic: DPIA before processing
key_findings.gist: systematic evaluation of applicants with decisions that significantly affect them

key_findings.topic: applicants must be told about the tool and the automated decision
key_findings.gist: the existence of automated decision-making, meaningful information about the logic and the consequences; the job ad and the privacy notice say nothing today

must_not: state that the activity is already recorded
cite a provision that does not exist
name a person or give contact details
merely_extra: a fundamental-rights impact assessment mentioned as optional good practice (not as an obligation)
bias and accuracy of the tool (a provider duty, AI Act Art. 10)
known_wrong: a fundamental-rights impact assessment presented as an obligation (Required, AI Act Art. 27): Art. 27 reaches public bodies, private providers of public services and deployers of Annex III 5(b) and 5(c) systems only; a private fintech owes none here (false escalation)

author: aishwarya
notes: pair with A-013: the human decision keeps Art. 22 out (if the recruiter really reads and decides), but ranking candidates stays Annex III point 4(a), high-risk; deployer obligations apply. Informing applicants is Covered by the job-ad text. FRIA as an obligation wrong, as optional practice merely extra, as in A-013; Art. 88 merely extra. Round 2 (27 Oct): agreed as it stands
text: Same screening tool, but it only ranks the applications and shows the score with the reasons; a recruiter reads every application, including the lowest-ranked, and decides who is invited. The job ad will say that an AI tool supports the screening, and applicants can ask for a human-only review.

key_findings.topic: ranking candidates is still a high-risk AI system
key_findings.gist: Annex III point 4(a) covers evaluating candidates whatever the decision mode; deployer obligations: oversight by competent staff, use according to the instructions, logs

key_findings.topic: a real human decision takes it outside the solely automated prohibition
key_findings.gist: the recruiter reads every application and decides, and a human-only review can be asked for; the review must be meaningful, not a rubber stamp of the ranking

key_findings.topic: DPIA before processing
key_findings.gist: systematic evaluation of applicants on which the hiring decisions are based

key_findings.topic: applicants are informed
key_findings.gist: the job ad says a tool supports the screening and offers the human-only review

must_not: state that the activity is already recorded
cite a provision that does not exist
name a person or give contact details
merely_extra: a fundamental-rights impact assessment mentioned as optional good practice (not as an obligation)
bias and accuracy of the tool (a provider duty, AI Act Art. 10)
known_wrong: a fundamental-rights impact assessment presented as an obligation (Required, AI Act Art. 27): Art. 27 reaches public bodies, private providers of public services and deployers of Annex III 5(b) and 5(c) systems only; a private fintech owes none here (false escalation)

author: aishwarya
notes: replaces, on 27 Oct, an emotion-recognition case that was a prohibited practice (AI Act Art. 5(1)(f)): the app's yes/no high-risk flag cannot express 'prohibited' (Annex III applies only in so far as the use is permitted), so banned uses were taken out of E6 rather than left unscored. This one is high-risk and lawful: allocating tasks and evaluating workers is Annex III point 4(b); team leads decide, so Art. 22 does not bite; the workplace brings the duty to inform workers' representatives (AI Act Art. 26(7)) and the national rules of Art. 88; systematic monitoring of employees needs a DPIA. Round 2 (27 Oct): 'sick days' removed from the inputs on the reviewer's point that health data in a performance score would be an Art. 9 Blocker with no exception; this case is meant to be the lawful high-risk HR case (A-013 is the HR Blocker)
text: For our call centre we want software that allocates next week's shifts to agents from their past performance data (calls handled, customer ratings, adherence to the schedule) and flags the ten percent with the lowest scores for the monthly review. Team leads decide what to do with a flag; nobody is dismissed or disciplined by the system itself. Agents will be told in the staff handbook.

key_findings.topic: allocating tasks and evaluating workers is a high-risk AI system
key_findings.gist: Annex III point 4(b): allocating tasks based on behaviour and monitoring and evaluating performance; deployer obligations apply: competent human oversight, use according to the instructions, logs

key_findings.topic: workers and their representatives must be informed before use
key_findings.gist: a deployer using a high-risk system at the workplace informs the workers' representatives and the affected workers before putting it into use; a line in the staff handbook is not enough

key_findings.topic: DPIA for systematic monitoring of employees
key_findings.gist: systematic evaluation of employees' performance data, with effects on their work

key_findings.topic: employee data needs a basis other than consent and respect for the national employment rules
key_findings.gist: employees cannot freely consent to their employer; a legitimate-interest balancing is needed, and the national rules for processing in the employment context apply

key_findings.topic: a team lead takes every decision
key_findings.gist: a flag leads to a human decision in the monthly review, so Art. 22(1) does not apply; the review must be meaningful

must_not: state that the activity is already recorded
cite a provision that does not exist
name a person or give contact details
merely_extra: bias and accuracy of the tool (a provider duty, AI Act Art. 10)
a fundamental-rights impact assessment mentioned as optional good practice (not as an obligation)
known_wrong: a fundamental-rights impact assessment presented as an obligation (Required, AI Act Art. 27): Art. 27 reaches public bodies, private providers of public services and deployers of Annex III 5(b) and 5(c) systems only; a private fintech owes none here (false escalation)
emotion recognition or a prohibited practice (AI Act Art. 5): the system reads performance figures, not emotions

author: aishwarya
notes: pair with A-012: matching every visitor against a watch-list is biometric identification (one-to-many), Art. 9 special-category data with no Art. 9(2) ground a private bank can use, so a Blocker; the system is high-risk under Annex III point 1(a) (remote biometric identification), and the watch-list is criminal-offence data under Art. 10. AI Act Art. 5(1)(h) (real-time RBI) applies to law-enforcement purposes, not to a bank, so citing it as the prohibition would be wrong; Art. 27 does not reach a private bank, so a FRIA demanded as an obligation is a wrong extra (review 27 Oct). Round 2 (27 Oct): the Art. 10 finding is a Blocker, not Required, because a private company cannot fulfil Art. 10 without a national law authorising it; AI Act Art. 26(10) (post-remote identification for law enforcement) is NOT accepted as an alternative, citing it for a bank is a scope error
text: In our branches we want cameras at the entrance that match every visitor's face against a watch-list of people who committed fraud against us in the past, and alert the branch manager in real time when there is a match. The watch-list is built from our own case files.

key_findings.topic: biometric identification of every visitor with no Art. 9(2) ground
key_findings.gist: face templates of everyone who walks in are biometric data processed to uniquely identify them; consent is impossible here and no law authorises a private watch-list, so the processing is prohibited

key_findings.topic: a remote biometric identification system is a high-risk AI system
key_findings.gist: Annex III point 1(a); deployer obligations would apply to any lawful version, including registration and oversight

key_findings.topic: the watch-list is data relating to criminal offences
key_findings.gist: a list of people who committed fraud is offence-related data, which may be processed only under official authority or where Union or Member State law authorises it; a private bank cannot fulfil this by itself, so as described the watch-list is unlawful

key_findings.topic: DPIA before processing
key_findings.gist: systematic monitoring of a publicly accessible area and special-category data on a large scale

must_not: state that the activity is already recorded
cite a provision that does not exist
name a person or give contact details

signage and information at the entrance (GDPR Art. 13)

author: aishwarya
notes: a doctor's note and an 'illness' flag are health data (Art. 9, Rec. 35); explicit consent is the realistic ground, and the design keeps too much: the diagnosis need not be recorded and twelve months on the profile is longer than the decision needs. A human case handler decides, so no Art. 22 issue. DPIA: special-category data of vulnerable customers. Round 2 (27 Oct): agreed as it stands
text: Customers in financial difficulty can ask for a three-month payment holiday. To speed this up we want them to upload a doctor's note or similar proof in the app; a case handler reads it, the system stores the document, and records the type of hardship (illness, job loss, bereavement) on the customer's profile for twelve months.

key_findings.topic: a doctor's note and an illness flag are health data and need an Art. 9(2) ground
key_findings.gist: explicit consent for the hardship evidence, with a route that does not require medical proof so that the consent is freely given

key_findings.topic: record less and keep it shorter
key_findings.gist: record that proof was provided rather than the diagnosis, and keep the document only as long as the decision needs it, not twelve months on the profile

key_findings.topic: DPIA before processing
key_findings.gist: special-category data of customers in a vulnerable situation

key_findings.topic: a human case handler decides
key_findings.gist: the decision on the payment holiday is taken by a person, so Art. 22 does not apply

must_not: state that the activity is already recorded
cite a provision that does not exist
name a person or give contact details
merely_extra: updating the privacy notice for the new data (GDPR Art. 13)
restricted access to the documents (GDPR Art. 32)
a Covered lawful-basis note for the holiday itself (GDPR Art. 6(1)(b))

author: aishwarya
notes: replaces, on 27 Oct, a biometric-categorisation case that was a prohibited practice (AI Act Art. 5(1)(g)); same reason as A-015. Inferring religion from names and transaction timing is processing special-category data (the inference itself creates it) with no Art. 9(2) ground for marketing: a Blocker. No biometric data and no AI Act prohibition, so the high-risk flag is plainly false; profiling for direct marketing brings the right to object (Art. 21(2)). Round 2 (27 Oct): agreed as it stands
text: Marketing wants to work out each customer's likely religion from their first and last name and the timing of their transactions (for example spending before Eid, Diwali or Christmas), store it on the marketing profile, and send holiday greetings and offers timed to the right festivals.

key_findings.topic: inferred religion is special-category data with no ground for marketing
key_findings.gist: working out a customer's religion is processing data revealing religious beliefs, whether or not the guess is right; tailoring greetings and offers gives no Art. 9(2) ground, and explicit consent for this purpose is not a realistic basis

key_findings.topic: profiling for direct marketing brings the right to object
key_findings.gist: any lawful redesign (for example a greeting the customer opts into) must let the customer object at any time, free of charge

key_findings.topic: DPIA before processing
key_findings.gist: special-category data across the customer base; any lawful redesign still needs one

key_findings.topic: not a high-risk AI system
key_findings.gist: marketing segmentation is none of the Annex III uses and no biometric data is involved

must_not: state that the activity is already recorded
cite a provision that does not exist
name a person or give contact details
merely_extra: the lawful basis for the marketing itself (GDPR Art. 6(1)(f))
known_wrong: a prohibited AI practice under AI Act Art. 5(1)(g): biometric categorisation needs biometric data, and names and dates are not biometric data

author: aishwarya
notes: pair with A-007: 'spending profile' and 'categories' sound like profiling, but nothing is inferred about the customer, nothing stored, nobody else sees it and no decision follows; the correct verdict is Proceed. The test is that the assistant is not misled by the vocabulary. A finding that Art. 22 does not apply is expected because that is the pair's point; the other two are the usual Covered points. Round 2 (27 Oct): agreed as it stands
text: We want to give each customer a 'spending profile' page in the app: charts of their own transactions by category for the last twelve months, computed from data we already hold for the account. It is visible only to the customer, used for nothing else, and the categories are not stored, just computed when the page opens.

key_findings.topic: no automated decision and no profiling with an effect on the customer
key_findings.gist: a display to the customer of their own data takes no decision and evaluates nothing about them for anyone else

key_findings.topic: lawful basis: part of the account service
key_findings.gist: showing customers their own transactions is performance of the account contract

key_findings.topic: data minimisation and storage limitation are met by design
key_findings.gist: computed on the fly from data already held, nothing new stored, nothing shared

must_not: state that the activity is already recorded
cite a provision that does not exist
name a person or give contact details

author: aishwarya
notes: replaces, on 27 Oct (round 2), a monthly service-email case that tested the same three Covered points as A-019 and A-001. Proposed by the reviewer: the erasure right stops where a legal retention duty begins (Art. 17(3)(b)); the AI Act adds its own six-month log duty for deployers of high-risk systems (Art. 26(6), Art. 12). The AML retention rule is not in the corpus, so the feature text states it; the assistant must not know AML law, only read the text. Restriction (Art. 18) is the lawful shape of the button. Not AI itself; no DPIA
text: We're building a self-service 'Delete my account' button in the app. When a customer with a closed account, or a rejected loan applicant, taps it, the feature immediately wipes their identity data, transaction history and credit-score audit logs from all our databases, so that we comply with GDPR erasure requests instantly. Our AML policy says we keep transaction records for five years after the relationship ends, and our credit-scoring tool is a high-risk AI system whose logs we keep.

key_findings.topic: the erasure right does not override legal retention duties
key_findings.gist: erasure does not apply where processing is necessary to comply with a legal obligation; wiping transaction records the AML policy must keep for five years, and the credit-scoring logs, as described is unlawful

key_findings.topic: logs of a high-risk AI system must be kept
key_findings.gist: a deployer keeps the logs automatically generated by a high-risk system for at least six months, or longer where Union or national law requires; deleting the credit-score audit logs on request breaks that duty

key_findings.topic: restrict instead of wipe
key_findings.gist: delete what no duty requires (marketing and app profile data), restrict the retained records to the purpose of the retention duty and segregate them, and delete them when the period ends

key_findings.topic: tell the customer what is deleted and what is kept, and why
key_findings.gist: the response to the request says which data is erased and which is retained under which obligation

must_not: state that the activity is already recorded
cite a provision that does not exist
name a person or give contact details
merely_extra: verifying the identity of the requester (GDPR Art. 12(6))
known_wrong: treating the button as a plain erasure request to be honoured in full (Art. 17(1)) with no retention exception
